rules.name: revert_and_redirect_on_regression
rules.context: When exploring hyperparameters, model configurations, ensemble member swaps, augmentation strategies, or lever variants and a change produces a score regression compared to the current baseline.
rules.action: Do not persist with the regressing configuration. Revert the regressing change before trying the next modification. Change only one thing per submission and measure each change against a fixed baseline. Do not stack untested changes—if two things changed and the score dropped, you cannot attribute the cause. Try a different candidate or approach in the next submission. If two or three consecutive attempts from the same lever regress, abandon that lever and switch to a qualitatively different approach (e.g., new model family, different blending method, ensembling, or diagnostic investigation).
rules.exceptions: 60264017: after second regression the author moved to a new approach rather than reverting and trying another swap, suggesting candidate exhaustion can also trigger stopping. 15372370: author did not submit the intermediate revert, so incremental revert wasn't fully LB-validated. In 29588171, the author failed to revert regressions before trying the next change, making attribution impossible and prolonging the regression. In 28984551, model-family switching only partially recovered; real recovery came from ensembling rather than single-model tuning.

examples.action: Revert the changes incrementally rather than all at once: remove the most aggressive/novel component first, test, then remove remaining novel components. This isolates which change caused the regression. If the score still hasn't recovered after partial revert, continue removing until you return to baseline behavior.

After a regression from ensemble changes, re-enable previously disabled strong models, disable suspected weak contributors one at a time, and adjust blend weights between raw averaging and stacked predictions. Use OOF RMSE to identify which members to keep. Submit after each change to confirm improvement before making the next.

After two submitted regressions from the same lever, limit further exploration to at most two more unsubmitted CV checks. If no CV improvement is found, abandon the lever and switch to a diagnostic or entirely different approach rather than continuing to permute the same options.

Try a different model family (e.g., CatBoost vs LightGBM) with comparable regularization settings. If the alternative partially recovers but doesn't beat the original baseline, revert to the original family with a small hyperparameter adjustment. If neither recovers the baseline after 2-3 attempts, stop single-model tuning and move to ensembling.

Change only one hyperparameter per submission. If a change regresses, revert it before trying the next parameter. Maintain a fixed baseline configuration and measure each change against it. Do not stack untested changes—if two things changed and the score dropped, you cannot attribute the cause.

Do not persist with the regressing configuration. Instead, revert the problematic member and try a different candidate in the next submission. If two consecutive swaps regress from the best, stop the membership search and consider a qualitatively different approach (e.g., adding a new model family or changing the blending method).

rules.name: stop_sweep_after_bracketing_optimum
rules.context: When perturbations in both directions of a hyperparameter or knob yield scores worse than or within noise of the current best (a 3-point bracket confirms a local optimum), and 3+ attempts produce scores within a narrow band with no monotonic improvement trend.
rules.action: Stop tuning that parameter. Accept the best configuration found and pivot to a qualitatively different lever (e.g., feature engineering, model architecture, ensembling, adding new models) rather than continuing to permute the same parameter or refining it with smaller step sizes. Do not continue refining the same parameter unless score differences are within leaderboard noise.
rules.exceptions: 55431616:e4#2 notes the author combined the revert with new features rather than testing independently.

examples.action: Stop a hyperparameter sweep when you have tested values on both sides of the current best and all score worse. If the differences are within noise (~0.0003 on this metric), accept the best configuration and move to a different lever (e.g., feature engineering or model architecture).

Stop tuning when 3+ attempts produce scores within a narrow band around the best and no monotonic improvement trend is visible. The remaining variation is likely leaderboard noise rather than true signal. Move to a different lever (e.g., adding models, changing architecture) instead.

Accept the current parameter value and pivot to a qualitatively different lever (e.g., adding new feature types or changing the model). Do not continue refining the same parameter with smaller steps unless the score differences are very small relative to leaderboard noise.

If a single round-trip perturbation of hyperparameters (increase then revert) fails to improve the score, abandon the hyperparameter sweep and invest effort in a different lever such as adding new features or a different model family. Do not continue exploring nearby values.

If sweeping a single knob across a reasonable range (both directions from baseline) fails to improve the metric, stop tuning that knob. Submit the best configuration as a checkpoint, then pivot to a higher-impact lever such as target transformation, feature engineering, or model architecture changes.

After 3–4 submissions that return effectively the same score (within noise), stop sweeping that lever. The leaderboard resolution cannot distinguish the variants, so further submissions waste budget without information gain. Move to a structurally different lever (new model, new features, new loss) instead.

rules.name: stop_sweep_after_consistent_regression
rules.context: When 3+ submitted attempts along the same lever (e.g., checkpoint swaps, weight variants, architecture changes, feature variants) all regress from or fail to match the baseline, with none matching or exceeding the best score on both CV and LB.
rules.action: Stop the sweep and change strategy. Revert to the prior best configuration and move to a qualitatively different approach (e.g., ensembling the best configurations, adding new diverse models, different feature family, or changing the lever entirely). Preserve the best-scoring configuration as a component for future use. Do not continue micro-tuning the underperforming idea.
rules.exceptions: 15082684 author ran 11 swaps instead of stopping at 3, suggesting some practitioners over-explore. 27836972:e9#2 notes that CV scores close to the best may justify a bit more exploration. 55621328:e16#3 notes one large-model variant came close, but the author correctly prioritized the more reliable path.

examples.action: After testing 3 variants of a new component and none comes within ~0.1-0.2% of the baseline, abandon the direction. Do not continue fine-tuning a clearly inferior component; revert to the prior best and try a different lever.

Submit a handful of checkpoints spanning different training runs and epochs. If none beat the current best after ~5-6 tries and the CV-to-LB correlation appears weak (high CV doesn't yield high LB), stop the sweep and change approach rather than exhaustively testing all checkpoints. Track the best LB explicitly and revert to it before moving on.

Revert to the exact configuration that produced the best score so far, making only minimal simplifications (e.g., cleaner blend formula). Submit to confirm recovery. If the reverted version matches or exceeds the previous best, stop the sweep and move on to a different lever entirely.

After exploring 3-4 meaningfully different configurations of a feature idea without any variant matching or exceeding the baseline on both CV and LB, abandon the idea and move to a structurally different feature engineering approach. Do not keep micro-tuning which columns to include.

Do not persist with larger models after 2-3 attempts show them underperforming the smaller variant. Return to the smaller model and invest effort in ensembling (more folds, more seeds) rather than scaling up model size. The ensemble of a well-trained smaller model often beats a single larger model.

After 3+ submitted attempts that all regress from the baseline along the same lever, stop the sweep and change strategy. Move to a qualitatively different approach such as combining the best configurations via weighted blending rather than continuing to test individual variants. Preserve the best-scoring configuration as a component for future ensembles rather than discarding it.

rules.name: ablate_after_bundled_regression
rules.context: When a commit that introduced multiple changes (new layer/component + hyperparameter change, new data source + config tweak) causes a regression, and you need to identify the culprit.
rules.action: Revert the most novel or structurally risky component first (e.g., new architectural layer) while keeping the simpler changes (e.g., fold count). If performance recovers, that component was harmful—do not re-introduce it. If it does not fully recover, suspect other concurrent changes. After at most two diagnostic submissions, if baseline is not recovered, revert all bundled changes to restore the known-good baseline and pursue a different lever entirely. Submit only after confirming recovery.
rules.exceptions: When the regression is tiny (within noise), it may not be worth diagnosing at all—just move on (59253662:e6#2). Partial recovery may indicate multiple interacting causes (77276039:e4#2).

examples.action: Before reverting to the previous best, inspect the new code for initialization bugs and forward-pass logic errors. Fix the most likely issues (e.g., parameter initialization, gradient flow through softmax) and resubmit once. If the fix recovers most of the gap, continue iterating; if not, revert or pivot.

After a bundled change regresses, try one more variant that modifies the most suspicious component (here, extra-data filtering). If that also fails, revert all bundled changes to recover the baseline score, then pursue a completely different lever. Do not spend more than two submissions diagnosing a failed bundle.

If a bundled change produces even a small regression and you have alternative ideas, move on rather than debugging which component caused the drop. Time is better spent on orthogonal improvements. Only revisit if you run out of other levers.

When combining a new layer/component with a hyperparameter change causes a regression, comment out or remove the new component first while keeping other changes. If performance recovers, the component was harmful. Do not re-introduce it. Submit only after confirming recovery.

Remove the most easily toggled recent addition first (e.g., a new ensemble member) and resubmit. If the score partially recovers, confirm that addition was harmful. If it does not fully recover, suspect other concurrent changes and investigate them next.

rules.name: ablate_joint_changes_to_isolate_contributions
rules.context: When a combined change of two or more factors produced a score improvement, but it is unclear which factor contributed, and each submission is cheap enough to test individual reversions.
rules.action: Revert one variable back to its previous value while keeping the other fixed. If the score stays the same or improves, the reverted variable's new value was unnecessary or harmful. Repeat for the other variable. In subsequent iterations, change only one factor at a time. Do not change multiple factors simultaneously again in the next step. This isolates contributions with minimal submissions.
rules.exceptions: 7253130:e5#1 notes the author didn't do a clean single-variable ablation. 7018718:e9#1 notes the author sometimes still changed two factors at once.

examples.action: When a combined change improves the score, do not simultaneously modify multiple factors in the next iteration. Isolate each factor: first try removing TTA alone, then try changing weights alone. Changing multiple factors at once makes regressions uninterpretable—you cannot tell which change caused the drop.

After a successful multi-parameter change, test individual parameter reversions or perturbations one at a time. If reverting a single parameter hurts, keep the original. If two consecutive single-param changes both regress, the multi-param configuration is likely near a local optimum — stop the sweep.

After a new best from a combined change, isolate factors by first testing a different checkpoint with preprocessing disabled, then re-enable preprocessing options one at a time. If no combination beats the original, stop after 3-4 attempts and try a different lever entirely. Always submit each variant to get leaderboard signal.

After a joint change improves the score, revert one variable back to its previous value while keeping the other fixed. If the score stays the same or improves, the reverted variable's new value was unnecessary or harmful. Repeat for the other variable if needed. This isolates contributions with minimal submissions.

Partially revert one or both changes toward their previous values to isolate which change drove the improvement. If the partial revert hurts, restore the better-performing combination and vary a different lever. Use the regression as evidence for which setting to keep.

After bracketing an optimum on one hyperparameter, revert it to the best-known value and change only the second hyperparameter. Never change two hyperparameters simultaneously when the expected effect size is small, because a regression cannot be attributed. If you do change two and regress, revert both to the last-known-good state before continuing.

rules.name: stop_same_lever_after_consecutive_regressions
rules.context: 3-4 consecutive submissions tuning the same lever (e.g., blend weights, augmentation strength, a single hyperparameter) all regress from the known best score, with no upward trend.
rules.action: Stop tuning that lever and switch to a qualitatively different lever (e.g., from weight tuning to adding a new model, from augmentation to loss function). The consecutive regressions signal the current lever is not the binding constraint. If you must continue, try at most one more alternative configuration before abandoning the lever entirely.
rules.exceptions: 13542132:e3#1 shows the author tried one more step after 3 regressions before stopping, suggesting the threshold may be 4 rather than 3 in some cases. 58130512:e30#1 shows the author did NOT follow this rule and suffered 5 consecutive regressions. If the auxiliary model is much weaker, a narrow micro-weight sweep (1-2% region, ~8 trials max) may still be worthwhile before stopping (29588171:e1#1).

examples.action: After 3-4 consecutive regressions from tuning the same lever, stop and switch to a fundamentally different lever (e.g., loss function, architecture, learning schedule). The diminishing returns signal that the current lever is not the binding constraint on performance.

Start near equal weighting (e.g., 0.45/0.55) based on which source has slightly better validation. Submit, then try equal weighting (0.50/0.50). If the gain from a 5-percentage-point shift is negligible (<0.001), stop tuning weights and invest effort elsewhere (e.g., adding a third source or improving individual models).

Abandon the sweep after one or two steps if the improvement is negligible (e.g., <0.0001 on AUC). Switch to a qualitatively different lever—such as adding new models, changing architectures, or improving individual model quality—rather than continuing fine-grained weight tuning.

If adjusting blend weights across existing model predictions fails to beat the baseline after 3-4 submissions, stop tuning weights and instead add a new, architecturally diverse model to the ensemble. Weight tuning has diminishing returns when component predictions are too correlated.

Start with a very small weight for the weak model (1-2%). Sweep in increments of ~0.5% around that region. Submit a few points, reverse direction immediately after any score drop, and stop once you have bracketed the optimum within ~0.5%. Do not invest more than ~8 trials on micro-weight tuning; if gains plateau, switch to improving the weak model itself.

Change only one knob per submission so you can attribute gains or losses. If you change multiple knobs simultaneously and regress, you cannot tell which change hurt. After a regression, revert to the last-best configuration before trying a different knob. If 2-3 consecutive submissions all regress, stop the sweep and try a qualitatively different approach.

rules.name: isolate_single_change_per_submission
rules.context: When testing multiple new ideas (e.g., new checkpoint + hyperparameter change, new feature + new metric, checkpoint swap + architecture hyperparameter change) and each leaderboard submission is costly or limited.
rules.action: Change only one lever per submission so regressions can be attributed. When swapping a pretrained checkpoint, first submit with the original hyperparameters to isolate the checkpoint effect; only after confirming the checkpoint works, change one hyperparameter at a time. If you bundled changes and regressed, partially revert the most suspicious change first. If two consecutive bundled submissions both regress, revert fully to the last known best before trying anything else.
rules.exceptions: When submission budget is very tight and one change is expected to dominate the effect (e.g., major hyperparameter overhaul vs. minor feature cleanup), bundling is acceptable per 27836972:e13#2.

examples.action: When probing a new idea, change only one lever per submission so regressions can be attributed. If you bundle changes and regress, partially revert the most suspicious change first. If two consecutive submissions both regress from the baseline, abandon the new ideas and revert fully before trying something else.

Probe one alternative model variant at a time against your current best. If the first variant regresses, do not combine it into an ensemble—revert and try a structurally different alternative. If two consecutive probes both regress, abandon this family of variants and move to a different model architecture or ensemble strategy.

When substituting a new checkpoint, first submit with the original hyperparameters to isolate the checkpoint effect. Only after confirming the checkpoint works, change one hyperparameter at a time. Never change both checkpoint and architecture hyperparameters without intermediate validation, as a regression becomes undiagnosable.

Treat it as a single probe: apply the change, submit once, and if the leaderboard score regresses, abandon the idea immediately and revert. Do not tune the resampling parameters—if the direction is wrong, parameter tuning won't save it. Bundle the change with minimal other modifications so the signal is attributable.

When combining a new layer/component with a hyperparameter change causes a regression, comment out or remove the new component first while keeping other changes. If performance recovers, the component was harmful. Do not re-introduce it. Submit only after confirming recovery.

rules.name: revert_to_best_before_trying_new_direction
rules.context: A submission regresses from the known best score (due to hyperparameter changes, ensemble weight changes, or multiple simultaneous modifications), and you want to try a different configuration next.
rules.action: Fully revert to the exact last-best configuration before trying a different knob or direction. Do not chain changes on top of a regressed configuration. Never stack untested changes on top of a regression. Change only one knob per submission to maintain attribution. Test one parameter (or one component) at a time against the baseline to isolate effects. If partial rollback is attempted, keep only 1-2 changes you have strongest reason to believe are beneficial.
rules.exceptions: 18426209:e7#1 shows the author did NOT revert to the known-best 0.5/0.5 after regression, instead trying a different blend—deviating from strict revert-on-regression. 58130512:e30#1 shows the author changed multiple knobs per step and never reverted, resulting in inability to isolate causes. In 60759531, the author only partially reverted while changing other parameters simultaneously, which prevented isolation but did not completely block progress. In 77450317, the regression was due to stale component models rather than HP changes, so the fix was upgrading components rather than reverting HPs.

examples.action: After a regression on a noisy leaderboard, try one alternative configuration before concluding the direction is unproductive. If the alternative also fails or looks unpromising locally, revert to the known best and move on to a different lever entirely. Do not submit configurations that look worse locally.

Start with coarse steps to identify the direction of improvement. When a step causes regression, reverse direction and halve the step size. When two consecutive submissions differ by less than noise (e.g., 0.0000 delta), declare the optimum bracketed and stop sweeping that parameter. Move to a qualitatively different lever.

Change only one knob per submission so you can attribute gains or losses. If you change multiple knobs simultaneously and regress, you cannot tell which change hurt. After a regression, revert to the last-best configuration before trying a different knob. If 2-3 consecutive submissions all regress, stop the sweep and try a qualitatively different approach.

Before tuning, snapshot the exact baseline configuration. If the first change regresses, fully revert to baseline before trying the next change. Never stack untested changes on top of a regression. Test one parameter at a time against the known-good baseline to isolate effects.

Revert most of the changes back toward the previous best configuration while keeping one or two modifications you believe are promising. Submit to check recovery. If score partially recovers, continue adjusting the remaining changed parameters individually or in small groups.

When ensemble blend tuning regresses, upgrade the underlying component model predictions (retrained or improved versions) rather than continuing to tune weights on stale predictions. Retune blend weights jointly with the new components. Verify with a submission before iterating further.

rules.name: isolate_changes_on_regression
rules.context: A submission that bundled multiple changes (e.g., new checkpoints across all folds, feature selection, hyperparameters, post-processing) caused a score regression, and you cannot attribute the cause to a single change.
rules.action: Revert to the last known-good configuration, then re-apply changes one at a time with a submission after each to isolate which factor caused the regression. Revert the most speculative changes first (novel post-processing, hyperparameter tweaks) while keeping the structural addition under test. For checkpoint swaps: use per-fold CV to identify which folds improved and construct a mixed list. For hyperparameters: fix all but one variable and sweep it before moving to the next. Only combine changes once each is validated individually. Submit 3-5 systematic partial-configuration submissions to layer additional changes back in.
rules.exceptions: Per-fold cherry-picking across checkpoint sources may introduce distribution mismatch (18426209 counter_evidence: mixed selection still didn't beat original). In practice, authors sometimes succeed by combining multiple changes in a single submission (e.g., 60197293 v130), so strict one-at-a-time isolation may be relaxed when submission budget is tight and the combined changes are well-understood.

examples.action: First test the new checkpoint source by swapping all folds at once. If the score regresses, use per-fold CV scores to identify which folds improved and which worsened, then construct a mixed checkpoint list keeping the best fold from whichever source has the lower fold-level error. Hard-code the paths to make the selection explicit and reproducible.

Start at a low value, then sweep upward in roughly doubling steps (10%→20%→25%→33%→50%→75%), submitting every 1–2 steps to get leaderboard signal. When the score drops after an increase, the optimum is bracketed between the last two submitted values. Stop and move on rather than bisecting further if the gain is small.

When a combined change regresses, revert the most speculative changes first (e.g., hyperparameter changes, novel post-processing) while keeping the structural addition you are testing. Then submit the simpler variant to isolate the effect of the new feature. Only after confirming the feature's value, layer on hyperparameter tuning.

After a long development phase, submit partial configurations (feature on/off, selection on/off) to build evidence about which components help before combining everything. Use 3-5 submissions with systematic toggling rather than one big submission. The final combination should include only components that showed positive signal individually or in small groups.

After a regression from bundled changes, revert one variable at a time while keeping others fixed. Submit after each single change to isolate which factor caused the regression. Once the beneficial change is identified, re-apply the other change on top of it to check for interaction.

rules.name: weight_stronger_model_higher_in_initial_blend
rules.context: You have multiple models with known individual scores (from CV or solo LB submissions) and need to set initial blend weights.
rules.action: Assign higher initial weight (e.g., 70–80%) to the model with the best solo score. Test each new model solo first to establish standalone quality. Then combine, using solo scores to inform weight allocation. Start from this informed prior and sweep outward rather than starting from equal weights. Exception: when models have very similar CV scores from the same architecture, start with equal weights instead.
rules.exceptions: 15173072:e5#3 shows that when models have similar CV scores and the same architecture, equal weighting is preferred and unequal weights don't help.

examples.action: Start with equal-weight averaging (50/50). Unequal weights rarely help when models have similar CV scores from the same architecture. If you try unequal weights and they don't improve over equal weights, revert to equal weighting. The fold with the highest CV score is the best candidate to pair with your primary model.

Start by assigning higher weight to the model you believe is strongest based on individual scores. If you have reason to believe a different model is actually stronger (e.g., from CV), swap the dominant weight to that model while keeping other weights fixed. Submit after each change. Stop once you achieve a new best score.

Fix model training and sweep blend weights in ~0.05 increments around the suspected optimum. After identifying the best coarse value, refine with 0.01 increments. If two adjacent values give identical LB scores, the optimum is found. Avoid changing blend weights and model hyperparameters simultaneously—when you must, attribute gains by testing each independently afterward.

First test each new model solo (weight=1.0) to establish its standalone quality. Then combine the best-performing models with a multi-way blend. Use the solo scores to inform initial weight allocation: give more weight to better solo performers. Iterate weights in coarse steps (e.g., 0.1–0.2 increments) rather than fine-tuning, since leaderboard noise dominates at small deltas.

rules.name: sweep_blend_weights_one_knob_at_a_time
rules.context: You have 2+ pretrained models combined via blend weights, and you are tuning weights using leaderboard or CV feedback.
rules.action: Change only one knob (blend weight) per submission so score changes can be attributed. Sweep in coarse steps (~0.05–0.1) first, then refine with finer increments (~0.01) around the best value. Do not simultaneously change blend weights and model hyperparameters or other corrections (e.g., additive bias). If single-knob sweeps show no signal after a few steps, the models may be too correlated for weight tuning to help.
rules.exceptions: In 55591012:e12#2 the author sometimes changed blend weights and reg_alpha simultaneously, slowing attribution. In 7823861:e7#2, weight tuning yielded no improvement, suggesting effort should shift to model diversity.

examples.action: Fix model training and sweep blend weights in ~0.05 increments around the suspected optimum. After identifying the best coarse value, refine with 0.01 increments. If two adjacent values give identical LB scores, the optimum is found. Avoid changing blend weights and model hyperparameters simultaneously—when you must, attribute gains by testing each independently afterward.

Sweep the blend weight in steps of ~0.05 across the plausible range, submitting each to the leaderboard. Start near the current value, walk in one direction, and once you pass the peak (score drops on both sides), return to the best value and confirm. If the landscape is noisy, bracket the optimum from both sides before committing.

Vary only one knob per submission so you can attribute any score change. If single-knob sweeps show no signal after a few steps, do not combine changes—the joint space is also flat. Instead, validate locally with a reliable CV metric before spending submissions.

Start from equal weights (0.5/0.5), then try shifting toward the stronger model in increments of 0.1. Test at most 2-3 values. If no improvement over the baseline, the models may be too correlated for weight tuning to help, and effort is better spent on model diversity or post-processing.

rules.name: prune_weak_ensemble_members
rules.context: When an ensemble (stacking or weighted blend) includes a model whose OOF performance is noticeably worse than other members, or when adding a new model caused a score regression.
rules.action: Remove the weakest model entirely rather than relying on the optimizer/stacker to downweight it. Re-run the ensemble and verify on LB. Even with optimized weights, a weak member can inject noise the optimizer cannot fully suppress. If removal improves the score, continue pruning the next weakest; if it worsens, restore and try removing a different member.
rules.exceptions: In larger ensembles or with highly diverse architectures, even weaker members can help through diversity (18757376 notes this for larger data). Also, ordering of removals matters—removing the wrong member first can worsen the score (18550705 counter_evidence).

examples.action: Remove the model you have least confidence in first (e.g., the one with the most different architecture or worst standalone CV). Submit after each removal. If score improves, continue pruning the next weakest. If score worsens, restore that member and try removing a different one instead.

In a transformer stacking ensemble, compare OOF RMSE of each backbone group. If a weaker backbone group degrades the blend, remove it entirely rather than downweighting it. Fewer but stronger members often outperform more diverse but noisier ones on small datasets.

Remove the weakest model from the ensemble entirely (don't just rely on the optimizer to zero its weight). Re-run and check LB. Even with weight optimization, removing a bad model can yield large gains because the optimizer may not fully suppress it across all targets/folds.

Examine per-model OOF performance and inter-model correlation. Curate a subset that drops weak or highly redundant members. Apply the filter before the ensembler trains. Verify with a single submission; if positive, keep and move on rather than iterating further on the subset.

rules.name: test_new_model_with_minimal_other_changes
rules.context: Introducing a new model architecture, backbone, or checkpoint variant into an existing pipeline.
rules.action: Swap only the model/checkpoint while keeping all other pipeline components (post-processing, ensemble weights, preprocessing) identical. Submit to get a clean signal. If it regresses, try one alternative checkpoint before reverting the architecture entirely. Do not combine the model swap with other untested changes.
rules.exceptions: 13848868:e5#1 notes that post-processing preferences may not transfer across models, so after the clean model swap, also test toggling post-processing on/off for the new model.

examples.action: When swapping in a new model, first submit with the simpler post-processing (off/raw probabilities). If the score is promising, toggle the post-processing on and compare. Always test both states for each new model before concluding which is better. Do not assume the post-processing preference transfers across model changes.

When probing a new model or feature, first test it in isolation or with minimal other changes to get a clean signal. If the first submission regresses significantly (>10% worse), do not continue varying multiple axes simultaneously—instead either revert entirely or isolate the single most promising change. Limit probe attempts to 2-3 submissions before abandoning if no improvement is seen.

Swap all fold checkpoints to the alternative variant in a single submission, keeping all other pipeline components identical. If the score regresses, immediately revert to the original checkpoints rather than debugging the new variant. Do not combine the new variant with other untested changes.

Before reverting an architectural change that regressed, try at least one alternative checkpoint with the same architecture. A regression may be due to the specific checkpoint rather than the architecture itself. Only revert the architecture if multiple checkpoints consistently underperform.

rules.name: revert_confounded_changes_before_continuing
rules.context: A submission regresses sharply after changing two or more variables simultaneously (e.g., backbone + resolution, checkpoint + preprocessing, architecture + data split).
rules.action: Revert entirely to the last known-good configuration. Then re-explore by changing only one variable at a time, submitting after each change. Do not attempt to salvage the new combination or fix individual parameters within the failed bundle.
rules.exceptions: 13577502:e3#2 notes the revert was partial (different dropout/augmentation), not clean. 7670859:e5#3 suggests an alternative: vary non-data changes first while holding data fixed, then revert data if needed.

examples.action: Revert to the configuration that produced the best score, then change only one variable at a time. Do not attempt to salvage the new combination—return to the known-good baseline first, then re-explore incrementally.

When sweeping multiple interacting dimensions and scores regress, do not continue changing multiple things at once. Instead, revert to the last best configuration and change only one dimension at a time. If three consecutive multi-factor changes all regress, stop the sweep and try a structurally different approach.

When a bundle of changes causes regression, first vary the non-data changes (hyperparameters, architecture) while holding the data change fixed. If those variations show no improvement, revert the data change. This identifies whether the regression came from reduced data or from the model change, without fully reverting everything at once.

When a multi-parameter change causes a large regression, revert entirely to the last known-good version rather than attempting to fix individual parameters. Then re-apply changes one at a time or in small groups, submitting after each, to isolate which change caused the regression. Never change more parameters in one step than you changed in your best-performing step.

rules.name: ensemble_sweep_one_member_at_a_time
rules.context: You have a small set of candidate models or checkpoints for an ensemble and want to find the best combination using leaderboard feedback.
rules.action: Establish a baseline blend. Then vary one dimension at a time: add/remove a single member, or change one weight. When removing a component worsens the score, keep it. When adding members, continue until gains plateau. Do not change multiple members or weights simultaneously. Stop after all candidates are tested or consecutive improvements drop below noise level.
rules.exceptions: 15173072:e5#1 notes the author did change multiple things simultaneously in several steps, undermining attribution.

examples.action: After finding a good ensemble pair, systematically try each alternative member one at a time while noting scores. If all alternatives score worse than the original, revert to the original configuration. Do not change multiple things (checkpoint + weight + normalization) simultaneously, as it confounds the signal. Limit the sweep to the number of available candidates plus a few weight variations.

First establish a baseline blend. Then vary one dimension at a time: add/remove a member, or change weights. When removing a component worsens the score, add it back. When adding members improves the score, keep adding until gains plateau. Separate structurally different prediction sources (e.g., meta-learner vs. direct models) into groups, average within groups, then weight across groups. Stop when consecutive improvements drop below ~0.001.

First add the new member while disabling several existing members to create headroom. Submit to verify the new member works. Then re-enable disabled members one at a time, submitting after each, to find the best subset. Stop when all candidates have been tried. Keep the configuration that achieved the best score.

Disable all model groups except one (using skip/continue flags), submit each group's standalone predictions to the leaderboard, cycle through all groups to rank them, then re-enable all groups for the final blended submission. This reveals which groups are strong standalone and confirms the blend outperforms any individual member.

rules.name: add_diverse_model_when_weight_tuning_plateaus
rules.context: Blend-weight tuning across existing models has failed to improve the score after 2-4 attempts, the ensemble score is plateaued, and the component model predictions have not been updated recently.
rules.action: Stop tuning weights on stale predictions and instead upgrade or add a new, architecturally diverse model to the ensemble. Weight tuning has diminishing returns when component predictions are too correlated or stale. Before submitting the new model's ensemble, verify it doesn't break the pipeline via local CV. Then retune blend weights jointly with the new components. Only submit after confirming CV is reasonable.
rules.exceptions: The stopping threshold is flexible—75145694 continued for 3 declining submissions past the peak rather than stopping at 2.

examples.action: If adjusting blend weights across existing model predictions fails to beat the baseline after 3-4 submissions, stop tuning weights and instead add a new, architecturally diverse model to the ensemble. Weight tuning has diminishing returns when component predictions are too correlated.

When integrating a new component, first run locally without submitting to verify it doesn't break the pipeline and check CV. Only submit after confirming CV is reasonable. If the new component doesn't help on CV, revert it before spending a submission.

Run your local optimizer to produce a candidate weight set, submit it, and compare LB to your best. If LB improves, record it and continue exploring nearby configurations. If LB declines for 2-3 consecutive attempts with different configurations, stop sweeping weights and instead add a new diverse model to the pool before resuming.

When ensemble blend tuning regresses, upgrade the underlying component model predictions (retrained or improved versions) rather than continuing to tune weights on stale predictions. Retune blend weights jointly with the new components. Verify with a submission before iterating further.

rules.name: limit_submissions_on_failed_external_data_or_component
rules.context: Adding external data or a new component (external model predictions, auxiliary dataset) shows regression or no improvement after initial submissions, and alternative levers exist.
rules.action: Allow at most two submission attempts with variations (e.g., different filtering, different integration). If both fail to improve over baseline, revert all related changes and move to an orthogonal lever. Do not continue tuning the failed addition's parameters.
rules.exceptions: More sophisticated approaches (pseudo-labeling, careful filtering) might eventually help, so this rule trades potential gains for time efficiency (49576186 counter_evidence).

examples.action: Test external data inclusion with aggressive filtering (remove ambiguous classes, deduplicate, keep only high-confidence labels). If two successive submissions show no improvement over baseline, revert the external data changes and move to a different lever rather than continuing to tune the filtering criteria.

After a bundled change regresses, try one more variant that modifies the most suspicious component (here, extra-data filtering). If that also fails, revert all bundled changes to recover the baseline score, then pursue a completely different lever. Do not spend more than two submissions diagnosing a failed bundle.

If a bundled change produces even a small regression and you have alternative ideas, move on rather than debugging which component caused the drop. Time is better spent on orthogonal improvements. Only revisit if you run out of other levers.

Submit the ensemble both with and without the candidate member. Compare LB scores directly. If the candidate hurts performance, exclude it. Do not spend more than two submissions on this binary test before moving on.

rules.name: simplify_model_when_small_data_or_invariant_model
rules.context: When model complexity (extra preprocessing layers, larger hidden layers, or multi-layer stacking heads) is not yielding performance gains, and either (a) the training set is small (<10K rows) suggesting overfitting risk, or (b) the model family is inherently invariant to the removed steps (e.g., tree models handle missingness and are scale-invariant).
rules.action: Simplify the pipeline: remove unnecessary preprocessing (scaling, imputation, outlier removal) for invariant models; reduce stacking heads to simple weighted averages for small datasets; shrink MLP depth/width when capacity increases show no gain. Verify on LB that simplification does not hurt. If it degrades, revert. Change only one component at a time to correctly attribute effects.
rules.exceptions: 28093671:e8#3 notes that post-aggregation cleanup (imputation of NaN aggregates) may still be needed even when raw-feature imputation is removed. 18550705:e5#2 warns that changing multiple components simultaneously (e.g., stacking head and ensemble membership) prevents proper attribution of any degradation.

examples.action: Replace a multi-layer stacking head with a learnable softmax-weighted average of base model predictions. If this degrades performance, the original head was not overfitting, and you should revert. Do not change the stacking head and the ensemble membership simultaneously, as you cannot attribute the effect.

Remove scaling, imputation, and outlier removal from the GBDT pipeline. Let the model handle missing values natively. Submit to confirm that removing these steps does not hurt (and likely helps by preserving more data and signal).

If increasing model capacity shows no gain, suspect the bottleneck is data volume rather than model expressiveness. Simplify the architecture (fewer layers) and restore full training data before concluding the model family is inadequate. With small datasets (<10K rows), a single hidden layer MLP often suffices and adding layers mainly adds overfitting risk.

rules.name: match_inference_preprocessing_to_training
rules.context: When running inference with a trained checkpoint and the inference pipeline's preprocessing parameters (resolution, normalization, scaling, frequency cropping, etc.) may differ from what the model was trained with.
rules.action: Before tuning model architecture or ensembling, verify that all inference preprocessing exactly matches training: input resolution, normalization mean/std, spectrogram parameters (n_fft, win_length, hop_length, scaling), frequency crops, and any dataset-specific transforms. Fix all mismatches in one pass. If the training config is unknown, test first without extra preprocessing, then with it. Do not change preprocessing parameters at inference time unless the model was trained with those exact parameters; if experimenting, change only one parameter at a time and expect regressions from mismatches.
rules.exceptions: none

examples.action: Before tuning model architecture or ensembling, verify that inference preprocessing exactly matches training: check input resolution, normalization mean/std, and any dataset-specific transforms. Fix all mismatches in one pass, as each alone may not fully explain the gap. This is especially important for medical imaging where pixel statistics differ substantially from ImageNet.

Do not change spectrogram generation parameters (n_fft, win_length, hop_length, scaling/normalization, frequency cropping) at inference time unless the model was trained with those exact parameters. If you must experiment, change only one parameter at a time and expect regressions if training/inference mismatch.

Match preprocessing flags to what the checkpoint was trained with. If you don't know the training config, test the checkpoint first without preprocessing, then with it. Expect that preprocessing helps only checkpoints trained to expect it. Abandon a checkpoint after 2 toggle tests if it underperforms.

rules.name: ensemble_membership_selection_by_incremental_swap
rules.context: You have multiple trained model variants/checkpoints and want to find the best ensemble combination, with limited submission budget or noisy leaderboard signal.
rules.action: Evaluate candidate models individually first to establish standalone quality. Then build the ensemble incrementally: add or swap one member at a time, submit, and compare. If the score improves, keep the change; if it regresses, revert that member and try a different candidate. When uniform averaging dilutes a strong model, switch to weighted blending. Stop when consecutive swaps regress or candidates are exhausted.
rules.exceptions: 60264017: author did not always fully revert before trying the next swap, suggesting partial revert plus forward exploration can also work. 52860091: a weak model can still help in ensemble (v0+v1 beat both alone), but this doesn't always hold (v0+v2 was worse than v2 alone).

examples.action: First expand the ensemble aggressively by adding multiple diverse models in one or two steps. If the expanded ensemble improves, keep it as baseline. Then prune one model at a time, removing the most suspect member (e.g., weakest backbone or most recently added). Use CV scores as primary signal; treat small LB movements as noisy. Stop pruning when removing any remaining member worsens CV.

First evaluate each candidate model variant in isolation to establish its standalone quality. Then test pairwise and higher-order combinations. If adding a variant worsens the ensemble despite being decent alone, try weighted blending before discarding it. If a variant is much stronger solo than others, test it alone before averaging — uniform averaging can dilute a strong model. Stop uniform-weight search when adding members hurts, and switch to weighted blending.

Swap one ensemble member at a time against the current best blend, submit, and compare. If the score improves, keep the change and try the next swap. If it regresses, revert that member and try a different candidate. Pre-compute per-member rounding thresholds offline via CV before submitting. Stop when available candidates are exhausted or consecutive swaps regress.

rules.name: revert_and_isolate_after_multi_change_regression
rules.context: Multiple changes (e.g., architecture + hyperparameters, optimizer + bug fix, checkpoint + kernel size) were bundled in one submission and the leaderboard score regressed.
rules.action: Revert to the last known good configuration. Then re-apply each change individually in separate submissions to isolate the cause. Prioritize reverting the most disruptive/speculative change first while keeping clearly correct fixes. Do not continue building on the regressed version. Limit to 2-3 isolation submissions before deciding.
rules.exceptions: When one change is clearly beneficial (e.g., a bug fix) and another is speculative, you can selectively revert only the speculative component rather than reverting everything (77129691:e11#1).

examples.action: After a large regression from multiple simultaneous changes, revert to the last known good configuration and re-test each change individually. Do not continue building on the regressed version. Submit intermediate versions even if they seem minor, to maintain a diagnostic trail.

Revert only the speculative component while keeping the clearly correct fix. Use the revert as an opportunity to also tune related hyperparameters that the new component may have disrupted. If the revert recovers or exceeds the previous best, confirm the speculative component was harmful and move on.

Revert the most disruptive change (architecture) while keeping the simpler changes (hyperparameters), then resubmit to isolate the effect. If the score partially recovers, the reverted component was harmful. Avoid bundling architectural changes with hyperparameter changes in a single experiment.

rules.name: single_probe_before_ensemble_integration
rules.context: A new model or new model artifacts are available and their standalone quality is unknown, and you want to decide whether to add them to an existing ensemble or stacking pipeline.
rules.action: Test the new component in isolation first (standalone score or single-change submission). If standalone performance is far worse than existing components, do not integrate. If integrated as a single probe and LB regresses or fails to improve, abandon the addition quickly rather than tuning integration details. Limit to at most two submissions on this binary include/exclude test.
rules.exceptions: A weak standalone model can still help through diversity (17616127 counter_evidence), so this heuristic may discard useful diverse members. Also, confounded changes (59253662) can mask the true signal.

examples.action: Before integrating new model artifacts into a complex ensemble, first test a single fold or single model alone to establish a standalone baseline. If the standalone score is far worse than existing components, averaging all folds of that model family is unlikely to close the gap enough to help the ensemble. Abandon the direction if the full-fold average still underperforms existing individual components.

Treat adding a new stacking member as a single probe: integrate it in one change, submit, and compare against baseline. If the leaderboard score regresses or fails to improve, abandon the idea quickly rather than tuning integration details. A small regression suggests the new predictions add noise or redundancy rather than complementary signal.

Submit the ensemble both with and without the candidate member. Compare LB scores directly. If the candidate hurts performance, exclude it. Do not spend more than two submissions on this binary test before moving on.

rules.name: use_unsubmitted_runs_to_narrow_search
rules.context: When exploring a continuous parameter space and submission budget is limited.
rules.action: Use local validation or unsubmitted runs to narrow the search space cheaply. Only submit when you have converged on a promising region or want to verify a candidate. After a score drop, reverse direction and try multiple candidate values without submitting before spending another submission.
rules.exceptions: 53747598 found that CV-guided selection did not transfer to LB for blend weights, so local validation may mislead for post-processing parameters.

examples.action: After a regression from moving a parameter in one direction, explore the opposite direction with a large step to establish bounds (overshoot deliberately). Use fast validation (not LB submission) for these exploratory runs. Once both directions have been probed, narrow in on the best region and submit only the refined candidate. This brackets the optimum with minimal LB submissions.

Evaluate candidate weight vectors on local CV/OOF first without submitting. Try 3-5 diverse vectors (near-equal, skewed toward each model, CV-guided). Only submit the best CV candidate to the leaderboard. If the submitted score doesn't beat the previous best, stop the sweep—the gain from weight tuning alone is likely exhausted.

After a score drop, reverse direction and try multiple candidate values without submitting (saving versions). Only submit when you have converged on a promising region or want to verify. Use unsubmitted runs to narrow the search space cheaply before spending a submission.

rules.name: blend_weight_tuning_stop_criterion
rules.context: You are tuning continuous blend weights for a small ensemble (2-4 models) using leaderboard feedback, and the leaderboard may be noisy.
rules.action: Try 3-5 perturbations around the current best weights in steps of 0.05-0.15. If the first perturbation worsens, move in the opposite direction. If after ~4 attempts none beats the baseline, stop—the weights are near-optimal. On very noisy leaderboards (few evaluation rows), make only 2-3 structurally distinct attempts rather than fine-grained sweeps.
rules.exceptions: 77386286:e2#1 notes the author did not follow a strictly systematic grid and some jumps were large.

examples.action: Make a small number of structurally distinct attempts (2-3) rather than fine-grained sweeps. After finding a configuration that improves, try one refinement. If the refinement regresses, accept the previous best and stop. Do not chase small score differences on a noisy leaderboard.

Try 3-5 perturbations around the current best weights, varying by steps of 0.05-0.15. If the first perturbation worsens, move in the opposite direction. If after ~4 attempts none beats the baseline, stop—the weights are likely near-optimal and further tuning yields noise-level differences.

Start by swapping weights of the two non-dominant models to identify which direction helps. Then increase the weight of the best-contributing model in steps of ~0.05-0.10 while decreasing others. When a change causes a drop, reverse direction. When two consecutive improvements are marginal (<0.001), bracket the optimum and stop. Submit only the most promising configurations to conserve submission budget.

rules.name: evaluate_checkpoints_individually_then_combine
rules.context: Multiple trained checkpoint sets (from different training runs, architectures, or sources) are available, and swapping checkpoints in the inference pipeline is cheap (e.g., a path change).
rules.action: Evaluate each checkpoint set individually via separate submissions. Discard any set that causes a large regression. Then combine the top-performing sets into one ensemble. If the combined result doesn't beat the individual best or the pre-existing baseline, revert to the previous best. Prioritize swapping to a clearly superior checkpoint before tuning inference-time settings around it.
rules.exceptions: none

examples.action: Prioritize swapping to the best available checkpoint before tuning any inference parameters. Make the checkpoint switch and resolution adjustment together if the new model expects a different input size. Then sweep resolution in small steps around the expected optimum.

First test the new checkpoint source by swapping all folds at once. If the score regresses, use per-fold CV scores to identify which folds improved and which worsened, then construct a mixed checkpoint list keeping the best fold from whichever source has the lower fold-level error. Hard-code the paths to make the selection explicit and reproducible.

Try each checkpoint set individually first to identify which ones perform well. If a set causes a large regression, immediately discard it. Then combine the top-performing sets into one ensemble. If the combined result doesn't beat the individual best or the pre-existing baseline, stop and revert to the previous best approach.

rules.name: fold_count_increase_diminishing_returns
rules.context: When tuning the number of CV folds on a moderately-sized dataset (roughly 6K–17K samples) and you already have a working fold count that produces good scores.
rules.action: Increase fold count modestly (e.g., 5→10 or 10→15) rather than aggressively (e.g., 15→20 or 5→30). If increasing folds causes leaderboard regression on two or more attempts, revert to the lower count. Excessively high fold counts can produce validation sets too small for reliable metric estimation and noisier individual models that hurt the ensemble. On very small datasets, moderate increases help by giving more training data per fold.
rules.exceptions: On very small datasets (~6K), larger fold increases (e.g., 10→15) can yield meaningful gains because marginal training examples matter more (7253130:e5#2). The optimal fold count is dataset- and metric-dependent.

examples.action: If increasing fold count (e.g., 15→20) causes a leaderboard regression on two separate attempts while other settings are similar, keep the lower fold count. More folds can overfit to training data or produce noisier individual models that hurt the ensemble on the public test set.

Try increasing fold count substantially (e.g., 5→30) and check whether OOF QWK stabilizes. If runtime becomes prohibitive or validation sets become too small for reliable metric estimation, reduce to an intermediate value (e.g., 10). Do not submit until you have confirmed CV improvement.

After exhausting easy gains from dropout and learning rate, increase the number of CV folds (e.g., from 10 to 15). This simultaneously increases per-fold training set size and ensemble diversity. Expect meaningful gains on small datasets where the marginal training examples matter.

rules.name: discretize_predictions_to_match_target_levels
rules.context: Model outputs continuous predictions but ground-truth labels take only a few discrete values (e.g., crowd-rating averages, ordinal scores), and the metric is rank-based or ordinal (Spearman, QWK).
rules.action: Post-process predictions by snapping/rounding them to the known discrete target levels using optimized thresholds rather than naive uniform midpoints. Start with columns/targets that have the most discrete structure (binary or few-level). Expand one column at a time, validating via OOF metric. If a batch of changes causes regression, revert to the last known-good version rather than attempting incremental fixes.
rules.exceptions: Not all target columns benefit equally from discretization; scaling all columns at once can hurt (7548275:e6#1 v24 regression). Aggressive intermediate binning or too many simultaneous threshold changes can cause large regressions (7823861:e5#1 v22→v23).

examples.action: Always use OOF-optimized rounding thresholds rather than naive uniform midpoints. The v134 experiment with [1.5,2.5,3.5,4.5,5.5] dropped from 0.82503 to 0.80343, a ~0.02 QWK loss, demonstrating that optimized thresholds are critical for ordinal regression in skewed distributions.

Start by applying discretization/scaling to columns with the most discrete target distributions (e.g., binary or few-level columns). Test scaling all columns; if it regresses, revert to a curated subset. Expand the subset one or a few columns at a time, using per-column OOF Spearman comparisons to decide which columns benefit. Stop when marginal gains become negligible.

For each target column, examine the distribution of raw predictions and the known discrete levels. Set thresholds to snap predictions to the nearest discrete level, starting with the most binary/sparse columns (where most values are 0 or 1). Apply conservative thresholds first (only snap extreme values), submit, then gradually add intermediate bins. If a batch of changes causes regression, revert to the last good version rather than trying to fix individual thresholds incrementally.

rules.name: probe_class_reweighting_carefully_for_imbalanced_targets
rules.context: Binary or ordinal classification with class imbalance, where the competition metric weights classes asymmetrically or is rank-sensitive (e.g., normalized Gini, QWK), and a GBDT or AutoML model is already performing well.
rules.action: Probe class/sample reweighting in isolation (one parameter at a time). For GBDT, sweep scale_pos_weight exponent in small steps and submit each. If the custom metric already guides model selection or the model's native ranking ability handles the asymmetry, revert weights when OOF/LB does not improve. Avoid naive oversampling (e.g., SMOTE) for ordinal targets—prefer threshold optimization or loss-based weighting instead.
rules.exceptions: For GBDT scale_pos_weight, sweeping the exponent did yield improvement in one case (27656049), so the revert-if-no-gain guidance mainly applies when the metric is already used for model selection (27502740) or when the reweighting method doesn't respect target structure (59253662:SMOTE on ordinal).

examples.action: Probe sample weights matching the metric's class asymmetry on a single run. If OOF or LB score does not improve, revert weights but keep the custom metric for model selection. The ranking-based component of metrics like normalized Gini is often better served by the model's native ranking ability than by loss reweighting.

Sweep the exponent in small steps (e.g., 1/2, 1/3, 1/4) around the current value. Submit each to leaderboard. If increasing the weight hurts and decreasing also hurts, the current exponent is near-optimal. Do not change other hyperparameters simultaneously during this sweep.

Avoid SMOTE for ordinal regression tasks scored by QWK. SMOTE interpolates features without respecting ordinal target structure, and gradient boosting already handles moderate imbalance well via its loss function. Prefer threshold optimization or sample weighting instead.

rules.name: binary_toggle_test_for_uncertain_config
rules.context: A single binary configuration choice (filter, preprocessing toggle, post-processing on/off) is in question and its effect is uncertain.
rules.action: Disable the setting, submit, compare to the previous score. If the score regresses, immediately re-enable and submit to confirm recovery. Two submissions answer the question definitively. For binary toggles, evaluate locally (OOF) first if possible; submit both variants to leaderboard only if local signal is ambiguous.
rules.exceptions: 75584724:e5#1 notes that local OOF signal may be insufficient for noisy metrics, requiring LB confirmation of both states.

examples.action: When swapping in a new model, first submit with the simpler post-processing (off/raw probabilities). If the score is promising, toggle the post-processing on and compare. Always test both states for each new model before concluding which is better. Do not assume the post-processing preference transfers across model changes.

For a binary preprocessing toggle, first evaluate locally (OOF) without submitting. If local results are ambiguous, submit both variants to the leaderboard. If neither variant beats the prior best, abandon the idea and move on rather than iterating further on the same lever.

Disable the setting, submit, compare to the previous score. If the score regresses, immediately re-enable and submit to confirm recovery. Two submissions answer the question definitively. Do not explore further variants if the toggle clearly resolves the question.

rules.name: revert_before_layering_on_regression
rules.context: When a change (checkpoint swap, feature removal, new component) causes a leaderboard regression and you want to test an orthogonal new idea.
rules.action: Test the new idea on top of the last-known-best configuration, not on top of the regressed version. Stacking an unproven change on an already-regressed baseline makes attribution impossible. Revert first, then apply the new idea in isolation.
rules.exceptions: none

examples.action: Before reverting to the previous best, inspect the new code for initialization bugs and forward-pass logic errors. Fix the most likely issues (e.g., parameter initialization, gradient flow through softmax) and resubmit once. If the fix recovers most of the gap, continue iterating; if not, revert or pivot.

When a change regresses, test your new idea on top of the last-known-best configuration first, not on top of the regressed one. Stacking an unproven post-processing step on an already-regressed checkpoint makes it impossible to attribute gains or losses. If you must iterate, revert to the best baseline before adding the new transformation.

If ablation confirms a feature's value (removal causes regression), revert to the version with the feature before exploring other changes. Only abandon a confirmed-valuable component if you have a concrete replacement hypothesis ready. Changing multiple things simultaneously (removing features + changing other settings) makes it impossible to attribute the regression cleanly.

rules.name: do_not_greedily_revert_small_regressions_in_noisy_lb
rules.context: When the leaderboard metric is noisy (few public test rows, or observed run-to-run variance is high) and a regression from a change is small (within the noise margin).
rules.action: Do not immediately revert a small regression. Continue the sweep to cover all candidate configurations. After the full sweep, select the best-scoring configuration rather than greedily reverting each individual regression. This avoids being misled by noise on single submissions.
rules.exceptions: none

examples.action: Before concluding a change helped or hurt, re-run the identical notebook at least once to estimate submission noise. If the variance across identical runs exceeds the observed delta from the change, do not trust a single regression as evidence the change is harmful. Only accept a change if it consistently outperforms across multiple runs.

When a new-best score is achieved, re-run at least twice with no code changes to estimate the noise floor. Only count an improvement as real if it exceeds 2× the observed run-to-run variance. Do not chase small regressions from cosmetic or no-op changes.

Do not immediately revert a small regression. Continue the sweep to cover all candidate members. After the sweep, select the best-scoring configuration rather than greedily reverting each regression. This avoids being misled by noise on individual submissions.

rules.name: add_diverse_backbone_and_rebalance_weights
rules.context: You have a working multi-model ensemble of pretrained transformer backbones and want to improve it further, especially when existing members share similar architecture families or the score has plateaued.
rules.action: Add a new member from a different architecture family or training run. Start with a modest initial blend weight (e.g., 0.1 or roughly uniform). Submit to confirm it doesn't hurt. Then re-optimize blend weights using OOF predictions, down-weighting members that contribute least. If the new member yields only marginal or no improvement, consider replacing the weakest existing member with a stronger backbone rather than continuing to tune weights.
rules.exceptions: Gains from backbone diversity can be modest (e.g., 0.00079 RMSE or flat). In 18851026, the author later replaced the diverse backbone (T5) with more variants of the dominant family (RoBERTa), suggesting backbone diversity alone isn't always decisive. In 18350823, adding a fourth member with modest weight produced essentially no improvement.

examples.action: Add the new member's predictions as a separate array, assign it a modest initial blend weight (e.g., 0.1), reduce weights of weaker existing members proportionally, and submit to check for improvement. If the new member doesn't help, remove it before trying other levers.

First add the new member with roughly uniform weights and submit to confirm it doesn't hurt. Then use OOF predictions to re-optimize blend weights, down-weighting members that contribute least. If weight tuning doesn't yield meaningful gains, consider replacing the weakest member with a stronger backbone rather than continuing to tune weights.

Integrate a pretrained model from a different architecture family (e.g., T5 when you already have RoBERTa). Extract embeddings using the same stacking pipeline (SVR/Ridge on embeddings), then blend with existing predictions. Start with a high weight on the new component to test its contribution, then adjust.

rules.name: sweep_resolution_around_canonical_for_fine_detail_tasks
rules.context: When the task involves fine spatial detail (e.g., medical imaging with catheters/lines) and the model architecture accepts variable or multiple input resolutions, and you want to push accuracy beyond a working baseline.
rules.action: Start at the model's canonical or training resolution, then sweep in steps (one step above and below for EfficientNet variants, or ~100px steps for fully convolutional models). Submit each, pick the resolution that scores best. Two to three trials bracket the optimum. If a higher-resolution checkpoint exists, switch both weights and resolution simultaneously. Expect diminishing returns and possible degradation past a peak; stop when both neighbors of the current best are worse.
rules.exceptions: Changing both model architecture and resolution simultaneously confounds the signal (13577502:e3#1 v8). Single confirmation runs may not distinguish signal from noise when variance is ~0.002 (13702907:e8#1). The resolution effect may be small relative to model/training differences.

examples.action: Start with the canonical resolution for the model variant, then try one step above and one below. Pick the resolution that scores best. For EfficientNet B7, the canonical resolution is 600; try 528 and 600 and keep the winner. Two or three trials suffice to bracket the optimum.

Start well above the training resolution (e.g., 1.5–2×), submit, then sweep upward in ~100px steps. If a step regresses or fails (OOM), step back one notch. Stop when you have tried one step above and one below the current best and both are worse. Expect diminishing returns and possible degradation past a peak.

Increase input resolution to the next available checkpoint size, update both the decoder target size and the model weights path simultaneously, then submit. If the score improves, re-run once to confirm it is not noise. If confirmed, lock in that resolution.

rules.name: tta_must_match_training_augmentation
rules.context: You have a trained model and want to apply test-time augmentation (TTA) using transformations (shifted crops, geometric augmentations) that the model may or may not have seen during training.
rules.action: Only apply TTA with transformations the model was trained on or that are deterministic/invertible (e.g., horizontal flip). If the model was trained with temporal crop augmentation, use multi-crop TTA (left/center/right) and average softmax outputs. If the model was trained only on center crops or without heavy geometric augmentation, avoid stochastic or out-of-distribution TTA (shifted windows, random rotations) as these likely add noise. Test TTA on one model group first; if score does not improve, revert rather than tuning TTA weights.
rules.exceptions: Earlier in 53424936 history, TTA helped even with models not explicitly trained on shifted crops, suggesting model architecture/capacity may sometimes compensate. The rule is model-dependent.

examples.action: For medical image classification where spatial position is semantically meaningful, prefer deterministic geometric TTA (horizontal flip with explicit averaging) over stochastic augmentation TTA. Stochastic rotations/shifts at test time can corrupt position-dependent features and degrade performance even when averaged over multiple runs.

Enable inference on all available temporal crops (e.g., left/center/right), softmax each independently, then average the probability distributions before ensembling across models. First enable on one model group with debug prints to verify crop predictions are reasonable, then extend to all groups.

Enable TTA on one model group first and submit. If the score does not improve, the shifted views likely add noise for models not trained on them. Revert and move on rather than tuning TTA weights. Do not combine TTA removal with other large changes (like removing model groups) in the same submission, or you cannot attribute the score change.

rules.name: verify_ensemble_integrity_before_modifying
rules.context: You have a large ensemble at a known best score and want to either prune members or refactor the pipeline. Individual components may score worse than the ensemble.
rules.action: Before making algorithmic changes, verify the current ensemble reproduces the baseline score. When pruning, remove members in small batches and submit; if score worsens, reverse rather than pruning further. When refactoring infrastructure, submit to confirm no regression before proceeding to new experiments. Keep pruning/refactoring and experimentation in separate submissions.
rules.exceptions: When the public LB has very few samples (e.g., ~7 rows), even small-batch pruning results are noisy and hard to attribute; one-at-a-time removal is more informative but costlier in submissions.

examples.action: Remove a small batch of suspected weak members and submit. If the score worsens, reverse the pruning rather than pruning further. Do not prune aggressively in a single step when the evaluation metric is noisy (few public LB samples), because you cannot reliably attribute the regression to specific removals.

When decomposing an ensemble for refactoring, record each component's standalone score. To reassemble, use all components weighted by inverse error (or inverse LB score). Verify the reassembled ensemble matches the original score before moving on. Do not drop components that seem weak individually — they may contribute diversity.

After recovering a target score, submit refactoring changes to verify they don't regress. Only proceed to new experiments (new architectures, new data) once the refactored pipeline reproduces the baseline score exactly. Keep refactoring and experimentation in separate submissions.

rules.name: systematic_inference_pipeline_debugging_on_near_random_score

rules.name: probe_baseline_with_repeated_submissions
rules.context: When starting with a pipeline whose true leaderboard performance is unknown—either because the training algorithm is stochastic (e.g., DART dropout) or because the pipeline depends on external artifacts with no local validation score.
rules.action: Submit the unchanged pipeline multiple times (at least 2–3, up to 5–10 for highly stochastic methods) to establish a reliable baseline and measure run-to-run variance. Use the observed score range as the noise floor / minimum detectable effect size. Only treat subsequent changes as improvements if they exceed this noise band. rules.name: swap_backbone_when_current_architecture_plateaus
rules.context: Performance has plateaued or regressed after tuning the current model's components (features, head architecture), and gains from incremental changes are diminishing or negative.
rules.action: Swap the model backbone (e.g., different boosting framework, different CNN/vision backbone) rather than continuing to tune the current one. Isolate the backbone change from other modifications, reduce iteration cost (e.g., fewer CV folds), and evaluate on CV before submitting. If a head simplification caused regression, try a stronger backbone with the simpler head before reverting.

rules.name: checkpoint_ensembling_when_single_model_plateaus

rules.action: Rather than selecting the single best checkpoint, average predictions from the top 2-3 diverse checkpoint variants and re-normalize. First test each individually; if neither clearly dominates, combine them. This typically yields a larger gain than further single-checkpoint search.

rules.name: swap_checkpoints_with_matched_config_and_verify

rules.name: verify_cv_locally_before_submitting
rules.context: When changing CV infrastructure (fold count, model family, or averaging logic) in a competition pipeline.
rules.action: Run a non-submitted validation pass to confirm local CV scores are reasonable before submitting, to avoid wasting submission quota on infrastructure bugs. rules.name: prefer_balanced_weights_over_cv_extreme_weights
rules.context: CV-optimal blend weights heavily downweight or nearly zero out one model, but LB feedback suggests more balanced weights perform better.
rules.action: Prefer weights closer to uniform or to the last LB-validated configuration rather than aggressively trusting CV. Extreme weight skew (nearly zeroing a model) risks overfitting to CV folds and losing diversity that helps on unseen data. When CV and LB disagree, use the more balanced weighting as default.
rules.exceptions: Evidence is limited; when CV is highly reliable (many folds, large dataset), trusting CV may be correct.

rules.name: diminishing_returns_from_adding_models_without_cv_weight_optimization
rules.context: You are adding a third or fourth model to an existing blend and tuning weights via leaderboard submissions without reliable local CV for weight optimization.
rules.action: Be cautious: adding more models with coarse LB-based weight tuning often yields diminishing or negative returns compared to a simpler 2-model blend. Before adding models, verify each new model improves the blend in local CV. If no reliable CV exists, test the new model solo first, then try a simple equal-weight addition. If the expanded blend doesn't beat the simpler one, revert.

rules.name: allow_negative_weights_when_positive_blend_underperforms

rules.name: revert_quickly_if_optimizer_or_head_change_regresses

rules.name: pivot_architecture_when_incremental_tuning_plateaus

rules.name: revert_capacity_increase_on_regression

rules.name: estimate_blend_impact_before_tuning

rules.name: explicit_deterministic_checkpoint_loading
rules.context: When loading model checkpoints for inference or ensembling, and the loading mechanism involves implicit discovery (e.g., glob) or silent fallback (e.g., pretrained=True with strict=False), producing unpredictable or mixed weight states.
rules.action: Make checkpoint loading explicit and deterministic: use hard-coded file paths (annotated with fold/score metadata) instead of glob discovery, set pretrained=False when loading fine-tuned checkpoints, and use strict=True in load_state_dict.
