rules.name: linear_meta_learner_for_stacking
rules.context: When stacking multiple base model predictions (OOF) as meta-features and the meta-feature space is low-dimensional (handful to ~20 base model predictions), especially with limited training data.
rules.action: Start with a simple linear meta-learner (Ridge regression or LinearRegression) rather than nonlinear alternatives. Ridge is preferred over Lasso when you already perform explicit feature elimination. If a nonlinear meta-learner (e.g., RBF SVR) does not improve OOF score, revert to the linear model rather than tuning kernel hyperparameters.

rules.name: isolate_regression_by_ablation
rules.context: Combining components (models in ensemble, or multiple simultaneous changes) causes a significant score regression compared to individual components or the prior baseline.
rules.action: Immediately isolate by running each component alone to confirm individual quality. Check merging/integration code for bugs (e.g., incorrect concatenation, misaligned predictions). Only after confirming components work individually and integration logic is correct, re-test the combination. For multi-component changes, remove the most aggressive/novel component first, test, then continue removing until regression source is identified.

rules.name: batch_infrastructure_changes_before_submitting
rules.context: A new approach requires coordinated changes across multiple pipeline components, and intermediate states are broken or not meaningful to evaluate.
rules.action: Batch all prerequisite infrastructure changes without submitting. rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: test_candidate_model_solo_then_in_blend
rules.context: You have a new candidate model and an existing ensemble of proven models, and want to evaluate whether the candidate adds value.
rules.action: First test the candidate model solo (or with minimal blending) to gauge standalone quality. Then add it to the existing blend and compare. A weak solo model may still contribute diversity, so do not discard based on solo score alone—judge by the final blend score. If adding it worsens the blend despite decent solo quality, try weighted blending before discarding.

rules.name: stop_after_two_consecutive_null_or_regressing_probes
rules.context: Two successive probes of the same lever (e.g., escalating a hyperparameter, ablating components, or tuning a preprocessing toggle) both show no improvement or increasing regression.
rules.action: Revert to the best-known configuration and abandon that lever. Move on to an orthogonal lever rather than continuing to probe in the same direction. Do not spend more than two submissions confirming what two data points already show.
rules.exceptions: none

examples.action: After two null results from increasing a parameter in the same direction, revert to the original value and move on to a different lever. Do not continue escalating; the signal indicates the lever has no effect or the effect is below measurement noise.

rules.name: bundle_high_confidence_fixes_to_save_submissions
rules.context: Multiple fixes are identified where each has high confidence of being correct (e.g., matching known training settings like resolution and normalization), and submission budget is limited.
rules.action: Bundle all high-confidence fixes into a single submission rather than testing each independently. Only isolate changes when the direction of effect is uncertain or when you need to attribute improvement to a specific change.
rules.exceptions: Bundling makes attribution impossible; if one change could plausibly be harmful, test separately (15082684:e4#2 counter_evidence).

rules.name: checkpoint_and_move_on_after_clear_improvement
rules.context: A single experiment yields a clear new best score, and there are other orthogonal levers (new features, new models) to explore.
rules.action: Record the result with version logs documenting the baseline score, checkpoint the code, and move on to the next orthogonal lever rather than immediately grid-searching around the successful hyperparameters. Return to fine-tuning later if needed.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: ablate_ensemble_member_before_tuning
rules.context: An ensemble has multiple members and you suspect one is weaker or its contribution is uncertain.
rules.action: Disable the suspected weaker member and submit the remaining prediction to measure marginal contribution. If the single/reduced model matches or beats the ensemble, drop the weaker member permanently. If it regresses, restore the ensemble and tune the weaker member or seek better diversity sources instead.
rules.exceptions: 27502740:e4#2 notes that if blending same-framework models hurts, seek diversity from a genuinely different source rather than abandoning blending entirely.

Keep the blending infrastructure but change what you blend.

rules.name: retune_blend_weights_after_ensemble_composition_change
rules.context: The composition of an ensemble has changed (models added, removed, or retrained) and blend weights were tuned for the old composition.
rules.action: Re-probe the blend weight by shifting it moderately from the previous best (e.g., ±0.10). If the first probe improves, accept it; if not, try the opposite direction. One or two probes usually suffice. Do not over-tune on a small public leaderboard—if redistribution causes regression, revert to previous weights and invest in improving base models instead.

rules.name: verify_inference_changes_before_submitting
rules.context: A change affects all predictions at inference time (e.g., TTA, dropout, scaling) and submission budget is limited.
rules.action: Add per-sample debug prints or logging for the new inference path, run without submitting to inspect outputs for sanity (reasonable ranges, no degenerate values). Only submit after confirming outputs look reasonable. This avoids wasting submissions on broken inference.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: gate_risky_changes_on_local_cv
rules.context: When probing a fundamentally different model, architecture, or speculative preprocessing change whose impact is uncertain and leaderboard submissions are limited.
rules.action: Do not submit until local CV confirms the change is at least competitive with the current best. Fix runtime issues first, then evaluate on validation. Only submit after CV scores match or exceed the current LB baseline. If CV is disappointing, abandon the probe without burning a submission.
rules.exceptions: When local CV is unreliable (very small dataset, high CV-LB divergence), a direct LB probe may be necessary.

rules.name: retest_cheap_toggles_after_model_change
rules.context: When you have a cheap binary post-processing toggle (e.g., rank conversion, normalization flag) or a blending weight whose optimal value was previously established, but you have since changed the underlying model or ensemble composition.
rules.action: Re-test both states of the toggle (or previously discarded parameter values) after every model/ensemble change, as the optimal setting can shift. Submit both and keep whichever scores higher. Do not assume the previous winner carries over.
rules.exceptions: none

rules.name: abandon_speculative_probe_on_first_regression
rules.context: When a speculative preprocessing or data augmentation change (e.g., text cleaning on pretrained encoders, SMOTE oversampling) is tested as a single probe and the leaderboard score regresses.
rules.action: Revert immediately rather than tuning the parameters of the failed approach. If the direction is wrong on the first try, parameter tuning is unlikely to save it. Do not invest multiple iterations refining an approach that hurt initially.
rules.exceptions: If the regression is very small and confounded by other simultaneous changes, a second isolated test may be warranted.

examples.action: Treat it as a single probe: apply the change, submit once, and if the leaderboard score regresses, abandon the idea immediately and revert. Do not tune the resampling parameters—if the direction is wrong, parameter tuning won't save it. Bundle the change with minimal other modifications so the signal is attributable.

rules.name: swap_backbone_diversity_over_weight_tuning
rules.context: When fine-tuning ensemble blend weights yields diminishing returns (negligible or negative improvement) and the ensemble contains multiple models from the same architecture family.
rules.action: Stop tuning blend weights and instead swap the weakest-contributing member for a backbone from a different model family (e.g., replace a RoBERTa variant with DeBERTa). Architectural diversity typically yields larger gains than optimizing blend coefficients among similar models.
rules.exceptions: If a non-linear blending formula (e.g., power-mean) hasn't been tried yet, it may yield a quick marginal gain before switching to backbone diversity.

rules.name: ensemble_ablation_via_pruning
rules.context: When you have a complex ensemble with many weighted members and want to understand which components are actually contributing to performance.

rules.name: stop_sweeping_after_structural_change_reprobe
rules.context: When you have already extensively swept a hyperparameter, then made a structural change to the pipeline, and a single re-probe near the old optimum confirms improvement.
rules.action: Accept the re-probed value and move on to a different lever rather than re-sweeping the full range. Diminishing returns are likely since the prior sweep already mapped the landscape and the structural change is unlikely to have dramatically shifted the optimum.
rules.exceptions: If the structural change fundamentally alters the prediction distribution (e.g., adding a new model family to the ensemble), a broader re-sweep may be warranted.

rules.name: revert_extreme_parameter_and_pivot

rules.name: incremental_changes_avoid_consecutive_failures

rules.name: pivot_lever_when_score_range_negligible

rules.name: stop_meta_learner_tuning_pivot_to_base_models

rules.name: sweep_full_range_then_confirm_under_noise

rules.name: fix_infrastructure_before_judging_variable
rules.context: When a run fails or produces suspicious/broken output after changing an experimental variable (e.g., checkpoint, config).

rules.name: enumerate_then_ensemble_small_option_sets

rules.name: revert_immediately_on_clear_single_variable_regression

rules.name: resubmit_identical_to_estimate_noise
rules.context: Leaderboard score differences between configurations are small (comparable to or smaller than suspected evaluation noise), making single-submission comparisons unreliable.

rules.exceptions: Consumes submission slots; may degenerate into cherry-picking the best random score rather than genuine noise estimation (50376011 counter_evidence).

examples.action: After any significant score change, re-submit the identical code once to estimate leaderboard noise. If the re-run score is within ~0.005 of the original, treat the result as stable and proceed. If it diverges more, average mentally and be cautious about small subsequent changes.

Submit the same unchanged notebook multiple times (5-8 runs) to estimate the noise floor of the leaderboard metric. Then compare the best or median score of each configuration across multiple runs rather than relying on single submissions. Only declare a winner when the gap exceeds the observed noise range.

rules.name: toggle_transform_in_isolation_before_fixing
rules.context: A prediction transform (e.g., sqrt, power transform) or calibration step gave mixed or confounded signals about whether it helps, because other changes were made simultaneously.
rules.action: Test the transform in isolation by toggling it on/off with all other settings held constant. If removing it hurts, restore it immediately and treat it as a fixed component for subsequent tuning. Do not re-test unless the ensemble composition changes substantially. Note that rank-based averaging may implicitly replace calibration transforms.
rules.exceptions: When switching to rank-based averaging, calibration transforms become redundant since ranks replace raw probabilities (15164527 counter_evidence).

examples.action: Test the transform in isolation by toggling it on/off with all other settings held constant. If removing it hurts, restore it immediately and treat it as a fixed component for subsequent tuning. Do not re-test it unless the ensemble composition changes substantially.

After a regression from bundled changes, revert one variable at a time while keeping others fixed. Submit after each single change to isolate which factor caused the regression. Once the beneficial change is identified, re-apply the other change on top of it to check for interaction.

rules.name: reverse_direction_on_regression_then_reduce_step
rules.context: During a leaderboard hyperparameter or blend-weight sweep, a parameter change causes a clear score drop compared to the previous best.
rules.action: Immediately reverse the direction of the parameter change, moving back toward the last best value with a smaller step size. Do not explore further in the regression direction unless there is a strong theoretical reason. If the reversal recovers or improves the score, bracket the optimum within a narrow range and stop.
rules.exceptions: none

examples.action: Immediately reverse the direction of the parameter change. Move back toward the last best value, possibly with a smaller step size. Do not explore further in the direction that caused the regression unless you have a strong theoretical reason.

After bracketing a hyperparameter optimum, test an extreme value far from the optimum (e.g., 5× larger) to confirm the direction of effect. If it confirms, return to the bracketed optimum but vary a co-parameter (e.g., regularization strength range) to check for interaction effects. If the combined change yields a new best, adopt both.

rules.name: bisect_continuous_hyperparam_near_optimum
rules.context: You are sweeping a continuous hyperparameter (e.g., blend weight, regularization), large steps cause regressions, and moderate steps yield small gains, suggesting the optimum is nearby.
rules.action: Start with coarse steps to identify the improvement direction. When a step causes regression, reverse direction and halve the step size. When two consecutive submissions differ by less than noise, declare the optimum bracketed and stop sweeping that parameter. Move to a qualitatively different lever.
rules.exceptions: 18426209:e7#1 shows the author did not strictly follow bisection—after regression at 0.65/0.35, they tried adding a third model rather than reversing direction on the same two-model weight.

examples.action: Try shifting weight toward the model you believe is strongest in small increments (e.g., 0.5→0.65). If the LB score worsens, do not continue in that direction; instead try adding a previously-dropped model at low weight. If neither improves over the baseline, stop weight tuning and accept the prior best.

Start with coarse steps to identify the direction of improvement. When a step causes regression, reverse direction and halve the step size. When two consecutive submissions differ by less than noise (e.g., 0.0000 delta), declare the optimum bracketed and stop sweeping that parameter. Move to a qualitatively different lever.

rules.name: fix_pipeline_bugs_before_continuing_sweep
rules.context: During an ensemble tuning sweep, a model that should be strong performs unexpectedly poorly, or you discover a data/model mismatch (e.g., shape mismatch, dead code, preprocessing inconsistency).
rules.action: Stop the weight search. Fix the bug, then re-run the best-known ensemble configuration to get a clean baseline before further tuning. Do not continue optimizing weights on top of a buggy pipeline.
rules.exceptions: none

examples.action: When a model that should be strong performs poorly in the ensemble, inspect its data pipeline for shape mismatches or preprocessing inconsistencies before continuing the weight search. Fix the bug, then re-run the best-known ensemble configuration to get a clean baseline before further tuning.

When integrating a new component, first run locally without submitting to verify it doesn't break the pipeline and check CV. Only submit after confirming CV is reasonable. If the new component doesn't help on CV, revert it before spending a submission.

rules.name: confirm_multifactor_change_before_iterating
rules.context: You have made multiple simultaneous modifications (e.g., new model versions + new blend weights, or several HPs at once) and the notebook has stochastic elements.
rules.action: After a multi-factor change, re-run the notebook unchanged and submit to confirm the score before making further modifications. This separates the signal of the change from run-to-run variance. Only proceed to the next iteration after confirming improvement.
rules.exceptions: none

examples.action: Before tuning, snapshot the exact baseline configuration. If the first change regresses, fully revert to baseline before trying the next change. Never stack untested changes on top of a regression. Test one parameter at a time against the known-good baseline to isolate effects.

After a multi-factor change, re-run the notebook unchanged and submit to confirm the score before making further modifications. This separates the signal of the change from run-to-run variance. Only proceed to the next iteration after confirming improvement.

rules.name: match_inference_resolution_to_model
rules.context: When running inference with a CNN (e.g., EfficientNet) and the test-time image resolution must be chosen, especially when switching between model checkpoints of different sizes.
rules.action: Derive the test-time image resolution from the model's expected input shape (e.g., canonical resolution for the variant, or programmatically from model.input.shape) rather than hardcoding an arbitrary value. Mismatched resolution can cause significant score drops (e.g., 0.957 → 0.945). When the model checkpoint changes, always update the resolution accordingly.
rules.exceptions: Auto-derived resolution may still produce poor scores if the model checkpoint itself failed to load correctly (13521245:e4#2).

examples.action: Start with the canonical resolution for the model variant, then try one step above and one below. Pick the resolution that scores best. For EfficientNet B7, the canonical resolution is 600; try 528 and 600 and keep the winner. Two or three trials suffice to bracket the optimum.

Derive the test-time image resolution from the loaded model's input shape (e.g., model.input.shape) rather than hardcoding it. This eliminates resolution mismatch errors when switching between model checkpoints of different EfficientNet variants.

Increase input resolution to the next available checkpoint size, update both the decoder target size and the model weights path simultaneously, then submit. If the score improves, re-run once to confirm it is not noise. If confirmed, lock in that resolution.

rules.name: hierarchical_blending_for_correlated_models
rules.context: When ensembling multiple model predictions where some sources are correlated (same architecture, similar training, or meta-learner trained on base model outputs) and others are more independent.
rules.action: Group correlated predictors into sub-averages first, then combine sub-group means at a second level using a separate weighted average. This prevents correlated models from dominating. Give groups with more diverse/independent predictions slightly higher weight. Do not simply append meta-learner predictions into the same flat averaging pool as base models.
rules.exceptions: When public LB feedback is very noisy (e.g., 7 rows), further refinement within the hierarchical scheme may regress (18837555:e5#1). Optimal structure may require more than two levels when additional diverse components are added (17616127:e10#2).

examples.action: Do not simply append meta-learner predictions into the same averaging pool as base models. Instead, average base models within their group first, then combine the group mean with the meta-learner output using a separate weighted average. Give the base model group higher weight (e.g., 5/12 vs 4/12) since it aggregates more diverse predictions.

Group correlated predictors into sub-averages first, then combine sub-group means with equal weight. This prevents correlated models from dominating. Try a balanced split (roughly equal-sized groups), submit, then refine by adjusting within-group weights. Stop when a refinement regresses.

rules.name: expand_feature_set_before_engineering_interactions
rules.context: When a GBDT model uses a small manually-selected subset of available features and scores poorly, before investing in crafting interaction or derived features.
rules.action: Progressively expand the feature set by adding batches of unused features ordered by importance, validating each expansion. Simultaneously simplify unnecessary preprocessing (imputation, scaling, outlier removal) that GBDTs handle natively. Only after the feature set is comprehensive should you consider adding engineered interaction features.
rules.exceptions: When all available features are already included (as in 27836972:e9#1), expansion is not possible and interaction engineering becomes the natural next step—though it may still not help.

examples.action: Start with a broad set of interaction pairs, submit or validate, then systematically narrow: remove columns that hurt CV one at a time, try both raw-level and aggregated-level (last, mean) variants separately, and compare CV. If the broad set doesn't beat baseline, try subsets before abandoning. Keep only the minimal set that improves CV.

Progressively expand the feature set: first add the next batch of important features and submit to confirm improvement, then add more, and finally switch to automatic aggregation of all available features. Simultaneously simplify preprocessing (remove imputation, scaling, outlier removal) that the GBDT doesn't need, since these steps may discard signal or add noise.

rules.name: avoid_broad_feature_removal_from_regularized_gbdt
rules.context: When using a well-regularized GBDT (with feature subsampling, bagging, early stopping) and you suspect broad categories of engineered features (e.g., all max/min aggregations, or permutation-importance-flagged features) are adding noise.
rules.action: Do not manually remove broad categories of engineered features by name pattern or a single importance run. If a targeted exclusion regresses the score, revert it. Instead, if importance-based removal hurts, regenerate importance with a different seed/method, compare lists, and only drop features consistently ranked unimportant across runs. The model's built-in regularization handles most irrelevant features.
rules.exceptions: Feature-selection ratio tuning (e.g., keeping top 50%) can still help; the rule applies to categorical exclusion by feature-name pattern or a single noisy importance ranking.

examples.action: Do not manually remove broad categories of engineered features (max, min, shift) from a regularized GBDT—the model's built-in feature subsampling and early stopping handle irrelevant features. If a targeted exclusion regresses the score, revert it and keep all features.

Rather than simply dropping fewer features, regenerate the importance analysis (possibly with a different seed or method) and construct a new drop list. Compare the two lists to identify features that appear in one but not the other—these borderline features are likely the ones causing the regression. Keep those borderline features and only drop the consistently unimportant ones.

rules.name: sweep_feature_count_threshold_bidirectionally
rules.context: When using high-dimensional features (e.g., TF-IDF) with an importance-based feature count cutoff and the current cutoff already produces a competitive score.
rules.action: Sweep the feature count in both directions from the current value using a fixed step (e.g., ±500–1000). If both directions degrade the score, the current value is near-optimal—stop sweeping and move to a different lever (e.g., adding new raw features or toggling feature selection on/off). When adding new feature sources, test with and without feature selection enabled to determine if the selection list is too restrictive for the new features.
rules.exceptions: none

examples.action: Sweep the feature count in both directions from the current value using a fixed step (e.g., ±1000). If both directions degrade the leaderboard score, the current value is near-optimal—stop the sweep and move to a different lever such as adding new raw features.

First test the new features with feature selection enabled (to filter noise). If that underperforms, try without feature selection (letting the model see all new features). Compare both against the baseline without the new features. If the new features help only without feature selection, the selection list may be too restrictive. Adjust the feature count cutoff by small increments (±500-1000) to find the sweet spot.

rules.name: advanced_pooling_for_small_text_regression
rules.context: When fine-tuning a pretrained transformer (e.g., RoBERTa) for regression on a small text dataset (~2800 samples) and the current model uses simple CLS or mean pooling.
rules.action: Experiment with richer pooling strategies: attention-based pooling over last hidden states, or weighted hidden-layer pooling (initialize layer weights as zeros for uniform weighting after softmax, concatenate mean-pooled and max-pooled representations). Validate via CV before submitting. Note that these changes alone on a single model may not beat a diverse ensemble, and combining with layer reinitialization can regress if layers don't converge—revert reinitialization before discarding the pooling change.
rules.exceptions: Combined pooling + layer reinitialization regressed on LB in one case (18757376:e5#2). A single improved-pooling model did not beat a multi-variant ensemble (17371717:e3#2), suggesting architectural improvements to one model may not substitute for model diversity.

examples.action: Initialize hidden-layer weights as zeros (uniform weighting after softmax), apply softmax in the forward pass to ensure proper normalization, and concatenate mean-pooled and max-pooled representations across the weighted layers. Avoid initializing layer weights with random values, as this creates unstable gradients early in training.

Try adding attention-based pooling over the last hidden states and reinitializing the last N (e.g., 4) transformer encoder layers to the model's initializer range. Validate via CV before submitting, as these changes can hurt if the reinitialized layers don't converge properly with limited data. If LB regresses, revert the reinitialization before discarding the pooling change.

rules.name: curate_base_model_subset_for_meta_learner
rules.context: When a stacking meta-learner has access to many base-model OOF predictions of varying quality, and some may be noisy or redundant.
rules.action: Curate a subset of base-model predictions rather than passing all to the meta-learner. Use iterative feature elimination: drop each base model one at a time and keep the removal if OOF score improves. Validate by toggling the filter off; if LB drops, keep the filter. Weak or redundant members add noise the meta-learner may not fully ignore.
rules.exceptions: Benefit may be marginal (~0.001 in 75924487:e4#2); the meta-learner switch alone was insufficient without elimination in 73937748:e11#1.

examples.action: Start with Ridge regression as the stacking meta-learner on rank-transformed OOF predictions. Add iterative feature elimination (drop each base model, keep removal if OOF score improves). Then tune Ridge hyperparameters (alpha, fit_intercept, positive constraint) with Optuna. Prefer Ridge over Lasso: L1 sparsity is less useful when you already do explicit feature elimination, and Lasso tends to underperform on small meta-feature sets.

Curate a subset of base-model predictions to feed the meta-learner rather than passing all available columns. Validate by toggling the filter off; if LB drops, keep the filter. Weak or redundant members add noise that the meta-learner may not fully ignore.

rules.name: match_pooling_to_checkpoint_at_inference
rules.context: When you have multiple trained checkpoints that were trained with different architectural variants (e.g., mean+max pooling vs. mean-only pooling) and need to select the best inference configuration.
rules.action: Ensure the pooling strategy at inference matches the one used during training for each checkpoint. Sweep all valid (pooling, checkpoint) combinations and compare LB scores. If neither variant consistently wins, pick the one with the best single result and refine checkpoint choice within that variant. Do not mix a checkpoint trained with one pooling type with a different pooling type at inference.
rules.exceptions: Sweeping a small number of combinations may be incomplete; the best combination may require a checkpoint not yet available (17371717:e13#1).

examples.action: Alternate between the architectural variants, each time loading the checkpoint that was trained with that variant. Compare LB scores across all combinations. If neither variant consistently wins, pick the one with the best single result and refine the checkpoint choice within that variant.

Try adding attention-based pooling over the last hidden states and reinitializing the last N (e.g., 4) transformer encoder layers to the model's initializer range. Validate via CV before submitting, as these changes can hurt if the reinitialized layers don't converge properly with limited data. If LB regresses, revert the reinitialization before discarding the pooling change.

rules.name: revert_or_restore_after_catastrophic_infrastructure_regression
rules.context: An infrastructure or dependency refactoring (not a modeling change) causes a catastrophic score drop (>10% or near-random), and a single corrective attempt does not fully restore performance.
rules.action: Revert to the last known-good version immediately rather than continuing incremental patches. Diagnose the root cause offline before re-attempting the refactoring. If the drop was caused by intentional ablation for diagnostics, keep the pre-ablation code intact (commented out) so restoration is trivial, complete the diagnostic sweep, then restore in one step.
rules.exceptions: If the drop is from an intentional diagnostic ablation (not a real regression), do not panic-revert — complete the investigation first, then restore.

examples.action: If a dependency or infrastructure refactoring causes a large regression and one corrective attempt does not fully restore performance, revert to the last working version immediately rather than continuing to patch. Diagnose the root cause offline before re-attempting.

Do not panic-revert after a catastrophic drop caused by intentional ablation. Complete the diagnostic sweep, then restore the full pipeline in one step. Keep the pre-ablation code intact (commented out) so restoration is trivial.

rules.name: revert_large_feature_batch_after_regression
rules.context: A large batch of new features was added and the leaderboard score regressed, and one or two compensating tweaks (loss tuning, postprocessing) fail to recover the prior best.
rules.action: Revert the feature addition entirely rather than continuing to tune around it. Do not spend more than two recovery attempts. If you believe some features are valuable, add them in smaller subsets in future experiments.
rules.exceptions: 55987255:e24#1 suggests that if you can confirm value by ablation (removing only the new features causes regression), keep them—but if recovery attempts fail, revert.

examples.action: Add the full feature pipeline in one commit, submit to get a leaderboard signal, then if the score improves, keep it; if you want to verify the contribution, remove only that feature block and re-submit. If removal causes regression, the feature is confirmed valuable—restore it rather than leaving it removed.

After adding a large feature batch, submit immediately to measure impact. If the score regresses and one or two small compensating tweaks (loss tuning, postprocessing) fail to recover the prior best, revert the feature addition entirely rather than continuing to tune around it. Do not spend more than two recovery attempts.

rules.name: quick_feasibility_probe_before_model_family_swap
rules.context: The current model family has plateaued or regressed despite hyperparameter tuning, and you want to try a fundamentally different approach.
rules.action: Run a quick probe with the alternative model on a small number of folds without submitting. Check that the model is compatible with the task (e.g., regression vs classification) and produces valid predictions. If the probe fails or produces clearly worse results, revert immediately. Keep the probe to one or two versions before deciding.
rules.exceptions: 7676170:e4#1 warns that hasty probes can miss fundamental mismatches (e.g., using a classifier for regression); verify task compatibility before coding.

examples.action: Before reverting an architectural change that regressed, try at least one alternative checkpoint with the same architecture. A regression may be due to the specific checkpoint rather than the architecture itself. Only revert the architecture if multiple checkpoints consistently underperform.

Run a quick probe with the alternative model on a small number of folds without submitting. Check validation output for basic feasibility (does it even produce valid predictions for the task?). If the probe fails or produces clearly worse results, revert to the previous model family immediately rather than tuning the new one. Keep the probe to one or two versions before deciding.

rules.name: estimate_noise_before_trusting_deltas
rules.context: When the effect size of a change is similar to or smaller than suspected run-to-run variance (e.g., identical or near-identical re-runs show score fluctuations comparable to the delta from a change).
rules.action: Re-run identical code at least once to estimate submission noise. Only accept a change as real if its improvement exceeds 2× the observed run-to-run variance. Do not chase small regressions from cosmetic or no-op changes.
rules.exceptions: This consumes submission budget; the author in 13542132 never achieved actionable conclusions because the re-run strategy consumed budget without yielding clear signal.

examples.action: Before concluding a change helped or hurt, re-run the identical notebook at least once to estimate submission noise. If the variance across identical runs exceeds the observed delta from the change, do not trust a single regression as evidence the change is harmful. Only accept a change if it consistently outperforms across multiple runs.

When a new-best score is achieved, re-run at least twice with no code changes to estimate the noise floor. Only count an improvement as real if it exceeds 2× the observed run-to-run variance. Do not chase small regressions from cosmetic or no-op changes.

rules.name: change_one_variable_at_a_time_when_effects_small
rules.context: When the expected effect size of each change is small (differences ~0.001 or less) and you want to explore multiple hyperparameters.
rules.action: After bracketing an optimum on one hyperparameter, revert it to the best-known value and change only the second hyperparameter. Never change two hyperparameters simultaneously when the expected effect size is small, because a regression cannot be attributed. If you do change two and regress, revert both to the last-known-good state before continuing.
rules.exceptions: 73671444 used forward-exploration instead of bisecting, which is faster when many untested model variants are queued but risks missing a valuable removed component.

examples.action: Rather than reverting, add the next planned component and test it in isolation (solo weight=1.0). If the new component partially recovers the score, continue building the blend. This forward-exploration approach is faster than bisecting the regression when you have many untested model variants queued, but risks missing that a removed component (like postprocessing) was valuable.

After bracketing an optimum on one hyperparameter, revert it to the best-known value and change only the second hyperparameter. Never change two hyperparameters simultaneously when the expected effect size is small, because a regression cannot be attributed. If you do change two and regress, revert both to the last-known-good state before continuing.

rules.name: move_on_after_quick_win_from_weight_tuning
rules.context: When a small adjustment to blend weights yields a new best score but the gain is modest and the weight space has limited remaining search space.
rules.action: After a quick win from blend weight tuning, move on to exploring new model components, architectures, or features rather than exhaustively searching the weight space. The marginal gain from fine-tuning weights among a few models is small compared to adding a genuinely complementary model.
rules.exceptions: 18423958 author's subsequent model explorations (DistilBERT) performed worse, suggesting sometimes sticking with weight tuning is safer.

examples.action: After a short sweep (3-4 trials) that brackets but does not beat the baseline, stop the sweep and use the directional signal (which variant scored best most often) to guide the next training run rather than continuing to permute inference-only combinations. Resume with a fresh checkpoint trained under the best-identified variant.

After a quick win from blend weight tuning, move on to exploring new model components or architectures rather than exhaustively searching the weight space. The marginal gain from fine-tuning weights among a few models is small compared to adding a genuinely complementary model to the ensemble.

rules.name: prefer_fixed_weights_on_noisy_leaderboard
rules.context: The public leaderboard is computed on very few samples (e.g., <10 rows), making single-submission score comparisons unreliable, and you are considering data-adaptive or conditional blending logic.
rules.action: Prefer fixed blend weights over data-adaptive conditional logic. If a conditional strategy does not clearly beat the simple fixed-weight version, revert to fixed weights immediately. On noisy leaderboards, try one alternative configuration after a regression before concluding the direction is unproductive, but do not iterate extensively on conditional approaches.
rules.exceptions: none

examples.action: On small or noisy leaderboards, prefer fixed blend weights over data-adaptive conditional logic. If a conditional strategy does not clearly beat the simple version, revert to fixed weights immediately rather than iterating on the conditional approach.

If the alternative also fails or looks unpromising locally, revert to the known best and move on to a different lever entirely. Do not submit configurations that look worse locally.
